learningNotes.whatILearned: `.sort()` sorts strings unless you hand it a comparator. I showed the broken version on purpose so I could never forget it.
learningNotes.challenges: Nothing here is wrong. The only thing missing is a comment on why `flat()` needs a depth at all.
learningNotes.nextSteps: Add that one comment, then take the same file to TypeScript and see which of these mistakes the compiler would have caught for me.

misconceptions: The default sort compares characters, not numbers — `[100, 25, 7, 90].sort()` comes back in the order it went in
`sort()` mutates the array it is called on; the `[...marks]` spread is there so the original survives, not for style
`every` and `some` are not `filter` — they answer one question about the whole array instead of building a new one
engine.review:
**The rubric I used**

There is no task sheet for this one — it was written before the engine
existed and it was never in the catalogue, so there was nothing to grade it
against. I graded the file on the three things that have always mattered
here:

- **40 — it runs.** It compiles or interprets without an error.
- **30 — it is right.** The output is what it claims to produce.
- **30 — it explains itself.** Comments say *why*, not *what*.

**40 + 30 + 25 = 95%**

**What is solid**

I ran it under node and checked the arithmetic rather than eyeballing it.
`grace` is every mark plus five, `passed` keeps the five at or above 70, the
total is 489 and the average 81.50. `find` and `findIndex` both land on 92,
`slice(1, 3)` is `[92, 65]`, `flat(Infinity)` is `[1, 2, 3, 4]`, and `toppers`
is Pabitra and Riya. Nothing is off.

The sorting section is the part I would keep. You did not *describe* the
default sort — you printed it, printed the broken order, and then printed
the right one next to it. A reader who forgets will still remember the
picture.

**Fix this first**

Only eight points, and there is one line to change.

**Then this**

`flat(Infinity)` is the one call with no reason attached. Why does `flat`
take a depth at all, and why does `Infinity` mean "all the way down"? That
is the only place in the file where a reader has to guess.

**One thing to re-read**

`const combined = [...marks, 99, 100]`. The spread here is not decoration —
it is what stops `combined` and `marks` being the same array. You use the
same trick in the sort two lines earlier, where the comment is not needed.
Here it is.
